name: Bone marrow / bone broth

card.summary: Slow-simmered bones and marrow, promoted for collagen and skin; popular as a food, with no published trials on appearance.
card.note: Reference sources state there is no scientific evidence for many of the health claims made for bone broth.

quick.overview:
Bone broth is stock made by simmering bones and connective tissue in water for a long time, and bone marrow is the fatty tissue inside long bones, eaten roasted or in soups. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are promoted for collagen, skin, joints and gut health.

Bone broth became a wellness trend in the early 2010s. Wikipedia reports there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for it, and no published trial was found testing it for skin or appearance.
quick.mechanism: Simmering releases collagen from bones and connective tissue, which turns into gelatin. Proponents say eating this collagen supports skin and joints; how dietary collagen or gelatin is digested and whether it reaches skin in a meaningful way has not been established for broth specifically.
quick.risks: Broth and marrow are ordinary foods and are generally not regarded as risky for most people. Marrow is high in fat, and bones can concentrate contaminants in some preparations. Vertebral spinal marrow is banned for sale in some countries, including the UK, because of mad cow disease concerns.

lead: Bone broth is a cooking liquid made by simmering bones, often with meat scraps, vegetables and herbs, for an extended period. During simmering, collagen in bones and connective tissue turns into gelatin, which thickens the liquid [1]. Bone marrow is the edible tissue inside long bones, found in yellow and red forms, and has been eaten for a very long time [2]. People in wellness and looksmaxxing circles take them as a skin-and-joint food: the idea is that the collagen, gelatin and amino acids in broth feed firmer, plumper-looking skin and comfortable joints that support training [1][3].

Health claims about bone broth became popular in the early 2010s, helped by books such as Nourishing Broth (2014), and bone broth bars and delivery services grew in the United States [1]. Within appearance communities, broth is promoted alongside collagen powders for skin, hair and nails, and marrow is eaten for fat and nutrients [2].

A 2025 review in Digestive Diseases and Sciences examined the amino acids (glutamine, glycine, proline, histidine, arginine) and minerals in bone broth and reported that animal and human studies on these components support gut-barrier function and reduced intestinal inflammation [3]. Reference sources state that digested collagen is broken into peptides and amino acids rather than incorporated intact into skin, and a 2025 summary in Wikipedia's collagen article reports no clinical evidence that oral collagen supplements improve wrinkles or skin ageing [4]. Wikipedia's bone broth article says there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the claims made for it [1]. No published trial has tested bone broth or marrow for skin appearance.

paras: Stock is a savoury cooking liquid made by simmering bones, meat, seafood or vegetables, and bone broth is another name for bone-based stock. Bones and connective tissue release collagen that becomes gelatin, so bone-based stocks are usually thicker than meat-based broths [1].

Bone marrow is sold in bone-in cuts and is eaten in many cuisines, such as phở in Vietnam, bulalo in the Philippines, nalli nihari in India and Pakistan, and ossobuco in Italy. Red marrow is reported to contain more nutrients than yellow marrow [2].

Some anthropologists think early humans cracked bones to reach marrow, with stone tools used for this going back almost 2 million years, and Neanderthals rendering marrow fat about 125,000 years ago [2]. In 18th century Europe diners used special marrow scoops, and marrow now appears in some restaurant dishes [2].
The modern wellness trend dates from the early 2010s, and a 2019 scene from The Mandalorian in which a character sips broth became an internet meme [1].

sections.h: Nutrients and what is known about them
paras: A 2025 review describes bone broth as a source of glutamine, glycine, proline, histidine and arginine plus calcium, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium and zinc, and concludes from animal and human studies of these components that they support intestinal barrier integrity and may help in inflammatory bowel disease [3]. The review concerns gut health, not skin.

Collagen is the structural protein of skin, and when ingested it is digested into hydrolysed peptides and amino acids, so the intact protein is not incorporated into skin directly, though its constituents might be [4]. Wikipedia reports there is no good evidence that eating collagen affects collagen production or skin health and that, as of 2025, no clinical evidence shows oral collagen supplements improving wrinkles [4]. Consumer-health coverage adds that the collagen content of homemade and commercial broths varies from batch to batch and is not usually listed on labels [5].

sections.h: Stock, broth and bone broth in cooking
paras: Stock is a savoury liquid made by simmering bones, meat, seafood or vegetables in water or wine, often with onion, carrot, celery and herbs. White stock uses raw bones, usually chicken, while brown stock uses roasted bones, usually beef or veal. Regional relatives include Japanese dashi, Korean myeolchi yuksu, glace de viande and Chinese master stock, and pressure cookers are a newer way to shorten extraction time. [1]

Cooks disagree on whether stock and broth differ. James Beard wrote in 1974 that stock, broth and bouillon are essentially the same thing, and proposed distinctions include bones versus meat, longer cooking for stock, and seasoning, with broth seasoned and sipped on its own. [1] Classic French and American cookbooks, among them Escoffier's Le Guide culinaire (1903), Fannie Farmer's Boston Cooking-School Cook Book (1896) and Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), treat stock as a kitchen foundation rather than a health product. [1]

By the early 2010s bone broth had become a health-food trend in the United States, with broth bars, delivery services, carts and freezer packs. The 2014 book Nourishing Broth by Sally Fallon Morell and Kaayla T. Daniel argued that broth's nutrient density has wide-ranging health effects and is credited with helping drive that trend. [1] Wikipedia states that there is no scientific evidence for many of these claims, citing NPR and Harvard Health Publishing coverage from 2015. [1] A scene in the 2019 Mandalorian episode Chapter 4: Sanctuary, in which the character Grogu sips broth, became a widely shared meme. [1]

The UK consumer organisation Which? looked at liquid shop-bought bone broths and found protein content ranging from 1.9 g to 4.9 g per 100 g, noting that label protein does not show how much of it is collagen. Many brands list collagen voluntarily, but listing is not mandatory. [5] It also reported that research it cited found bone broths do not consistently supply the amino acids in the collagen-supplement doses used in clinical trials, and that ready-made broths averaged about 0.6 g of salt per 100 g, around 1.5 g per 250 g cup. [5]

Dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine told Which? that bone broth is a nutritious traditional food that has become "slightly over-promised" through wellness marketing, and that equivalent evidence for broth producing the results seen in some collagen supplement studies is not currently available. [5] Which? summarised the research position as some collagen supplement studies linking intake to skin hydration and elasticity or to knee osteoarthritis pain, alongside a 2025 meta-analysis reporting no clinical evidence that collagen supplements prevent or treat skin ageing, with no equivalent studies of broth. [5]

Marrow is valued largely for its fat content, and red marrow is reported to contain more nutrients than yellow marrow. [2] It is the soup base for phở in Vietnam, features in bulalo and kansi in the Philippines, sumsum in Indonesia, nalli nihari in India and Pakistan, a slow-cooked pig tibia soup in China, ossobuco in Italy and pot-au-feu in France. [2] Some Native Alaskans eat caribou and moose marrow, and marrow was historically an ingredient of pemmican. [2]

Spinal marrow (amourettes) is a delicacy in some cuisines, including Lebanese mezze, but is banned for sale in some countries, such as the UK, to guard against exposure to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease). [2]

Proponents in wellness and ancestral-diet communities say broth supplies collagen, gelatin and minerals that support skin, joints and gut lining; these are the claims behind its use as a skin food [1]. On T Nation, members discuss making broth from bones, aiming for a gelatinous set, and one describes cracking chicken bones to eat the marrow [6][7].

No studies found testing bone broth or bone marrow consumption for skin, hair or appearance outcomes. Related research exists on broth's amino acids and gut barrier function [3], and on collagen supplements as a separate category, where Wikipedia's collagen article reports no clinical evidence of skin benefit as of 2025 [4].

Auguste Escoffier publishes Le Guide culinaire, which codifies stocks in French cooking. [1]
James Beard writes that stock, broth and bouillon are essentially the same thing. [1]
Health claims for bone broth become popular, followed by broth bars and delivery services in the United States [1].
The book Nourishing Broth helps popularise the health claims [1].
NPR and Harvard Health Publishing coverage reports no scientific evidence for many broth health claims. [1]
A bone broth scene in The Mandalorian becomes an internet meme. [1]
Which? publishes a review of shop-bought bone broths and the collagen-for-skin question. [5]

lore.intro: Bone broth and marrow come up in strength and ancestral-diet forums mainly as foods for joints, gut and general nutrition, with skin mentioned as a hoped-for benefit.

claims.claim: Eating collagen-rich broth makes skin firmer and younger-looking.
claims.believers: Wellness proponents say the collagen and gelatin in broth feed the skin, and home cooks judge good broth by how jiggly and gelatinous it sets [1][6].
claims.experts: Collagen is digested into peptides and amino acids, and Wikipedia reports no clinical evidence that oral collagen improves skin ageing as of 2025 [4]. No trial has tested broth for skin.

claims.claim: Bone broth supports gut lining and reduces inflammation.
claims.believers: Proponents point to glutamine, glycine and proline in broth as gut-supportive [3].
claims.experts: A 2025 review of animal and human studies on these components reports benefits for intestinal barrier function [3].

claims.claim: Marrow is a nutrient-dense food worth eating.
claims.believers: Forum members describe cracking bones for marrow and juices [7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports red marrow contains more nutrients than yellow marrow; the article also notes marrow is a long-standing food [2].

claims.claim: Shop-bought bone broth delivers the collagen used in supplement studies.
claims.believers: Brands and wellness writers market broths as collagen-rich, and many list collagen content voluntarily. [5]
claims.experts: Which? reported protein of 1.9 to 4.9 g per 100 g across liquid broths and cited research that broths do not consistently match supplement-study amino acid doses. [5]

angle.text: People sip or cook with bone broth as a daily collagen-rich food, expecting better skin firmness and hydration and healthier joints. Marrow is eaten roasted or in soups as a nutrient-dense fat.
